title: The Knowledge and the Knower
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: Andrew Cantarutti starts from his students' discovery that a children's novel about the 1913 Karluk expedition replaced an eight-year-old Inupiaq girl, and the Inuit family whose skills kept the party alive, with a fictional white girl. He uses the case to argue that knowledge and the knower cannot be separated, drawing on Tim Ingold's idea of an education of attention and on Inupiaq words for sea ice. Such knowledge is contextual, tied to a place and season, and relational, held and protected by a community. He contrasts this with AI-research definitions of intelligence built around a single agent, given goals and interchangeable environments, and notes that language models ingest the written record, which is skewed toward English and omits most of what humans have known. He grants that machines can produce new knowledge, but warns students may conclude everything worth knowing is already written down. His conclusion is that schools should teach the knowledge and the knower, using Albert Marshall's idea of two-eyed seeing.
points: The novel's erasure of Kiruk, Keraluk and Qagguluk shows how stripping a skill from its context and community destroys the way it was known.
Ingold's education of attention frames knowledge as something a novice rediscovers under an elder's guidance, which makes it contextual and relational.
Common AI definitions of intelligence feature a singular agent with given goals and interchangeable environments, leaving out place and other people.
Abstraction can reason but cannot notice, and models trained on text hold the vocabulary of ice without the risk of standing on it.
Schools should teach both Indigenous and Western knowledge, and should teach students where knowledge comes from and who holds it, even as AI tempts them to close one eye.
quotes: The knowledge and the knower can’t be separated, and the reason why tells us something about what we mean by intelligence.

Abstraction can tell you what ice of a given thickness should be able to hold, but it can’t tell you that the ice in front of you this morning is different from what you saw yesterday. That kind of awareness requires physical presence. Abstraction can reason, but it can’t notice.
The machine ingests the record, not the whole of human knowledge.

In a world where novel discoveries may be relegated to artificial systems, students might come to believe that everything worth knowing has already been written down and only needs to be looked up. A child who believes that stops experimenting.
Schools have spent a long time pretending to have just one eye. Artificial intelligence vows to make that eye sharper, while incenting us to close the other.
Our students need to know where knowledge comes from, who holds and protects it, and how new knowledge is made, whether on the ice or in the classroom.
